title: What low-level design is
idea: Low-level design (LLD) turns a feature into concrete classes, interfaces, methods and the links between them, so the code is clear, testable and easy to extend.
points: High-level design (HLD) picks services, databases and how they talk.
LLD works inside one service: which classes exist and who owns what.
A good LLD lets you add a feature by adding code, not editing it.
LLD interviews ask you to model a small system and defend each choice.

items.label: Clarify
items.text: Ask what the system must do and what is out of scope.

items.label: Find nouns
items.text: Nouns in the use cases become candidate classes: `Room`, `Booking`, `Employee`.

items.label: Assign jobs
items.text: Give each class one responsibility and the data it needs to do it.

items.label: Draw links
items.text: Decide is-a and has-a links, then sketch a UML class diagram.

items.label: Define contracts
items.text: Put an `interface` where behaviour may vary, such as a pricing rule.

items.label: Code and check
items.text: Write the classes, run a scenario, and adjust names and links.

quiz.q: Which question belongs to low-level design rather than high-level design?
options: Should orders and payments be separate services?
Which class decides whether two bookings overlap?
Which database should store the bookings?
How many servers sit behind the load balancer?
quiz.why: LLD works inside one service: it decides which class owns a rule. Services, databases and servers are HLD choices.

takeaway: HLD picks the boxes; LLD designs the classes inside each box.
